chunks.text: The primary stage of wastewater treatment is the removal of both grit and primary sludge. Grit is represented in the model as solid-state silicon dioxide which is about 1% of the total inlet water flow. The grit in wastewater has a specific gravity in the range 1.5-2.7 kg/l which is much higher than that of the organic matter suspended in the influent stream (1.02 kg/l). A differential sedimentation can thus be a successful mechanism for separating grit from organic matter (Liu and Lipták, 2000) . A density-based classifier is defined as a unit operation to remove the grit in this model. The primary treatment can reduce the Total Suspended Solids (TSS) by 50-60%. Also, it implies the removal of the BOD in the incoming wastewater by 20-30%. The percentage of the sludge removal chosen in the present model is 55%.

chunks.text: Primary sedimentation is to remove the suspended solids (SS) by controlling the water flow velocity. It is required the settling time of SS shorter than the water travelling time in the tank. The SS with low density (1.1 g/mL and 1.5 g/mL) or small size but high density (1.5 g/mL) is the target pollutants to be removed in primary clarification. Most abundant MPs in the wastewater is PET followed by PE and PP (Fig. 2b ). The density of PET is between 0.96 and 1.45 g/mL. It is predicted that the primary sedimentation would catch the MPs consist of PET. However, PE and PP are difficult to be removed as they have density lower than water. Hence, wastewater containing large amount of moderate-density MPs would have high MPs removal during primary treatment.

chunks.text: The secondary clarifier is a 10-layer non-reactive system labelled from the bottom to the top. It has a total height of 4 m, and occupies a surface area of 1500 m 2 and a volume of 6000 m 3 . The tank is fed from the 6th, treated water is harvested from the 10th, and the settled sludge flows out from the first layer. A fraction of the sludge flows out of the system in the form of waste at a flow rate of 385 m 3 /d, corresponding to a biomass age of 9 days, while the other fraction is recycled externally to the first tank at a rate of 18,446 m 3 /d. The biological processes occurring in both biological reactors are simulated using the IWA Activated Sludge Model No. 1 (ASM1) proposed by [47] . This model uses thirteen state variables to track the fate of biodegradable, non-biodegradable, soluble, insoluble, nitrogen, and carbon materials. These state variables are linked to eight degradation bioprocesses occurring in biological reactors.

chunks.text: A pilot-scale system, consisting of a grit tank and microscreen for primary treatment followed by a SAF-MBR 2.0 for secondary treatment, was installed at the Codiga Resource Recovery Center (Stanford, CA), as illustrated in. The pilot-scale system treated municipal wastewater pumped from the Serra Street sewer on the Stanford campus for more than three years. Sewage was de-gritted in a grit tank then subject to primary treatment by screening through a 0.3 mm pore size microscreen (MS-28, Hydro International). The pilot-scale SAF-MBR 2.0 consisted of: (1) two AFBRs operated in parallel, hereafter referred to as AFBR 1 and AFBR 2, containing fluidized GAC biocarrier, and (2) a gas-sparged membrane tank equipped with ultrafiltration membranes. Recirculation of bulk fluid (twice the influent flow rate) between the three reactors enabled complete mixing and control of solids accumulation within the gas-sparged membrane tank.

chunks.text: Anaerobic digestion is a biological decomposition process used to treat, stabilise, and reduce the quantities of organic wastes prior to disposal or beneficial re-use. Anaerobic digestion has been used extensively in municipal wastewater treatment to stabilise primary sludge and activated sludge. Over the past decade, municipal wastewater treatment processes have adapted to meet reduced discharge limits on the effluent nitrogen concentration. Process adaptations include the removal of primary settlings and primary sludge streams; and increased retention times for biological nutrient removal (BNR) processes, resulting in increased sludge age. Increased sludge age results in waste activated sludge with inherently low degradability, as inert materials in the influent, as well inert decay products accumulate in the activated sludge (Gossett and Belser, 1982) . Adaptations of modern wastewater treatment processes have introduced new challenges for anaerobic digestion, as poor degradability of activated sludge requires long digester retention times, higher mixing costs, and also results in poor gas production. Incorporating a pre-treatment into anaerobic treatment may enhance the sludge digestion by accelerating hydrolysis, which is generally accepted as the rate-limiting step in anaerobic digestion.

Water flowrate, water quality, and biosolid characteristics were collected from the facility's Discharge Monitoring Reports. This included carbonaceous biochemical oxygen demand (cBOD), total nitrogen, total phosphorous for water emissions. Water quality data and ammonia discharge limit data for the case studies is provided in Table SI-3. It should be noted that all sites were regulated and in compliance to meet monthly (cBOD) and total suspended solids (TSS) emissions of less than 30 mg/L and 80 mg/L, respectively; whereas minimum ammonia emissions varied 0.22-13.7 mg/L depending on the receiving water body characteristics. These systems were designed based on regional design standards in the U.S. (GLUMRB, 2014) and are expected to be representative of most systems performing secondary treatment with similar water quality objectives. Biosolids were land applied to local agriculture land in all the case studies and included emissions of tested chemicals and heavy metals. For most sites, the quantity of biosolids being land applied was not available, and thus was estimated based on average rates observed at other sites and scaled for the respective flowrate.

chunks.text: Preliminary treatment is the initial stage where coarse particles and foreign matter commonly found in raw wastewater are removed to optimize subsequent treatment processes (Sonune and Ghate, 2004) . This stage involves activities such as coarse screening, grit removal, and the comminution of large objects in wastewater. Grit chambers maintain high water velocities, preventing organic compounds from settling within the chamber. Although not all wastewater treatment plants incorporate grit removal in their preliminary treatment, some employ comminutors alongside coarse screening to reduce the size of large particles. Additionally, flow measurement devices and wave flumes are commonly used during this phase (Pachwarya et al., 2021) . It's crucial to remove oil and grease from wastewater at this stage to mitigate its adverse effects on the subsequent treatment processes. This is typically achieved through methods such as chlorination, vacuum flotation, and aeration (Pachwarya et al., 2021) .

chunks.text: The main objective of primary treatment of wastewater is the removal of settleable organic and inorganic solids by sedimentation and skimming. Here, about 50 to 60% of the total suspended solids (SS), and 65% of the oil and grease are removed along with some organic nitrogen, phosphorous, and heavy metals attached to the solids. However, the colloidal particles and dissolved constituents are not removed in this stage. Generally, gravity separation is employed in this step to separate the biosolids using either coagulation, flocculation, flotation or filtration techniques as seen in Fig. 2 . However, recent innovations in efficient wastewater treatment have brought advancements in this area (Table 4 ). For example, Salsnes filter system reported to have only 1/10th of land requirement and offers 30-60% lower investment and operating costs as compared to a conventional primary treatment system (Trojan Technologies, 2012).

chunks.text: As shown in Fig. 4 , the process boundary starts with the primary treatment process removing large floating particles and coarse solids. The grit removal step removes sand, gravel, dust and similar suspended solids. Oil skimmers scoop off oil residues (Wahlberg et al., 2005) . The secondary treatment step, biological treatment, uses activated sludge, microorganisms and microbial aggregates to reduce the biochemical oxygen demand (BOD), chemical oxygen demand (COD) and suspended solids. In the aeration tanks, return activated sludge (RAS) from the clarifiers is used to decompose organic matter. Clarifiers also produce surplus activated sludge (SAS). SAS is sent to the sludge treatment process line. Up to 85% of BOD and total suspended solids can be removed after the completion of the secondary treatment process (Hsu et al., 2014) . The wastewater is then treated to the tertiary level using disc filters, ultraviolet (UV) filtration and chlorine disinfection. The amount of sludge generated from tertiary treatment is insignificant compared to that generated from secondary treatment (FAO, 2020). Sludge treatment aims to reduce the sludge volume by thickening, stabilization, conditioning, and dewatering.
